transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-02-05
Start time: 09:30 PST
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Amy Park (Redwood AE), Daniel Ortiz (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Alpine Data Eng), Roberto Salinas (Alpine ML Eng), Priya Iyer (Alpine Infra)

Summary:
Quick weekly POC sync focusing on staging access ramp, recent benchmark oddities at p99, and SLO tuning for promotion to canary. Agreed next steps: run larger throughput bench, share sample traffic, exchange network/CIDR info, and circulate security docs.

Topics:
- Staging infra readiness and access escalation
- Latency profile (p50/p95/p99) and tail spikes
- KV cache / prefix caching behavior and batching
- Private deployment networking (VPC, peering, egress)
- Security artifacts (SOC2, KMS, audit logs)
- Canary cutover window planning

Transcript:
[00:00] Amy: Alright folks, thanks for joining, we'll start in a minute. I think we have everyone, Maya, Roberto, Priya, yep?
[00:18] Maya: Yep, we're here. Good morning Amy, Daniel.
[00:21] Amy: Morning. Quick agenda — status from your side on staging access, any blockers, then Daniel will walk through the benchmark notes from last run, then security/network gaps. Does that sound right?
[00:33] Priya: Yep, good. We also have a small ask on SSO that I want to flag.
[00:36] Amy: Noted. Daniel, take it away on the perf notes.
[00:40] Daniel: Cool. So we re-ran the micro-bench on Friday with the batching knob at 8 and prefix caching on for KV, same model variant as before. The p50 looked good around 60ms, p95 at ~180ms, but we've still got occasional p99 spikes around 1.2s which is higher than our expectation. There were also a couple of requests that hit cold KV misses — I suspect the prefix cache TTL is too short for your traffic shape.
[01:12] Roberto: Yeah we noticed during the test a couple of the multi-turn flows do create a different prefix each time, so maybe the K-V cache keys are too specific. Can you clarify what you mean by prefix caching?
[01:26] Daniel: Sure. It's the automatic K-V prefix aggregation — Redwood will try to store shared KV states so subsequent requests can skip recompute. If your prompts mutate the system role or include per-user metadata inside context, it fragments the keys. So two suggestions: either normalize the prompts server-side or expand the prefix grouping TTL.
[01:48] Maya: Right — we're doing user-id embedding in the prompt for personalization. We can attempt to shift that out to metadata, but that's a moderate change. What's the effort on changing TTL?
[01:58] Daniel: TTL change is fast on our side; it's a config flip. But it trades memory for hit-rate. On a 4-GPU staging pool we saw an increase in memory usage ~15% when TTL was extended from 30s to 5 minutes.
[02:16] Priya: Memory on staging is fine but in prod we'd need a cost estimate. Also curious about your quantization path — the numbers seemed better on the quantized variant but some hallucinations cropped up in the generation tests.
[02:29] Daniel: Good callout. We ran both fp16 and int8 variants; int8 lowered latency by ~20% but did change token probabilities slightly which can affect hallucination. For this pilot I'd recommend fp16 in canary, int8 for cost experiments after acceptance.
[02:42] Amy: Also to add, the dedicated capacity SKU will let you pin memory profiles so the TTL memory tradeoff is more predictable. For the pilot we can stay hosted but with reserved burst capacity if you want.
[02:56] Roberto: Hmm, reserved burst capacity sounds useful. What's the trade vs Dedicated?
[03:00] Amy: Dedicated gives you isolated GPU pools and predictable throughput / unit economics; reserved burst in hosted is cheaper to start but you share runtime with other tenants which can introduce jitter under peak.
[03:10] Maya: That jitter is what we saw — most of our spikes corresponded to concurrent batch windows. Any way to smooth that?
[03:16] Daniel: We can adjust request shaping and jitter smoothing at the ingress router — also continuous batching parameters can be tuned to favor steady latency at the cost of some throughput. We should test a configuration tuned for low tail latency.
[03:30] Priya: Okay. On networking — we tried the VPC peering tests you sent earlier, one snag: our security team won't allow open egress to all outbound IPs. We need a small CIDR range to lock down.
[03:42] Amy: We can provide that. Daniel, can you include the minimal egress CIDRs and ports in the checklist?
[03:47] Daniel: Yes — I'll include the CIDR list and port 443 only. Also note for private deployment there's an option for direct fiber/partner on-prem but that's later.
[03:56] Maya: Also SSO — our infra wants SAML 2.0 with SCIM provisioning, is that supported?
[04:02] Amy: Yes, SAML + SCIM is supported for console access. For API keys we can integrate KMS-backed secrets through your KMS or Redwood's KMS-integration.
[04:13] Priya: On KMS — does Redwood support customer-managed keys / HSM? It's required for our compliance.
[04:18] Daniel: We support customer-managed KMS and can integrate with your cloud HSM for encryption at rest. There is an audit log export that can be routed to your SIEM as well.
[04:28] Roberto: Great. Regarding the benchmark logs you mentioned — can we get raw traces? We want to overlay with our app traces.
[04:33] Daniel: Absolutely. I'll upload the raw pcap-style logs and token-timestamp traces to the support share. I'll also annotate where we saw cache misses.
[04:40] Maya: Perfect. A couple of small transcript artifacts — we saw occasional 502s at the API gateway when the pool autoscaler spun up nodes. Any way to suppress that?
[04:49] Daniel: Those 502s were transient; we can add a soft-fallback to a compatible model variant when autoscaler events happen. That reduces user-facing errors but may change token cost slightly.
[05:02] Amy: For the canary cutover, would the customer prefer a gradual traffic ramp over two hours or a single low-traffic window?
[05:08] Priya: Gradual ramp is safer for us, our compliance group wants a 2-hour observation window at low traffic.
[05:13] Amy: Ok we'll plan for a ramped canary. I'll coordinate scheduling.
[05:17] Roberto: One last thing — we ran a small adversarial prompt suite and saw an increase in repetition when using int8 quant. I want that logged as a risk.
[05:25] Daniel: Noted — I'll put that in the bench notes as a qualitative regression.
[05:29] Maya: Timeline wise, if we get the sample traces to you tomorrow, when can we expect the benchmark run back?
[05:35] Daniel: If we get traces by EOD tomorrow, we can run a scaled 10k-token throughput run and share p50/p95/p99 and raw traces by Monday (2026-02-09).
[05:42] Amy: Great. I'll follow up with the calendar invites and we'll attach the checklist and SOC2 summary.
[05:48] Priya: For the SOC2 docs — an executive summary is fine first pass; if we need deeper artifacts we'll request an NDA.
[05:55] Amy: Understood. We'll send the summary and the KMS integration guide; Daniel will include the CIDRs.
[06:00] Roberto: Also curious: did you mention any competitors with similar private deployment flows? We evaluated Anthropic on a separate pilot but the network piece was trickier.
[06:11] Amy: Yes we often see Anthropic and Bedrock in evaluations; their private network flows vary, but Redwood's unified runtime aims to minimize differences between hosted/dedicated/private.
[06:22] Maya: Ok that's it from our side. Anything else?
[06:25] Amy: Nope. Quick recap of next steps and action items will be in the notes. Thanks everyone.

Recap / Action summary (auto-generated):
- Daniel: Run larger throughput bench (10k tokens) with prefix TTL extended; upload logs and mark cache miss points. Due 2026-02-09.

- Priya: Confirm network CIDRs and SSO/SCIM requirements. Due 2026-02-10.
